newsitem.title: UK: TENNIS-DAY FOUR SNIPPETS FROM WIMBLEDON.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-DAY FOUR SNIPPETS FROM WIMBLEDON.

text.p: Snippets from the fourth day of Wimbledon on Thursday:
Quote of the day - "The weather forecast is very depressing" - Tournament referee Alan Mills, unable to offer much encouragement after the first complete wash-out at Wimbledon since 1992.
Stat of the day - 88. The number of years since two whole days were lost to rain in the same Wimbledon fortnight.
Strawberry delight - Rain may have ruled out any tennis, but there was an entertaining encounter of another type taking place.
The venue was the press cafeteria as Mary Pierce and Mary-Joe Fernandez fought their way around the room pursued by hordes of demanding photographers.
The reason? They were called on to hand out strawberries to the press in an attempt to encourage some publicity on an otherwise dull day. - - - -

Big-match nerves - It's not only how to curtsy that worries some women players but when to curtsy and where. Australian Rachel McQuillan, who lost 6-0 6-2 to Monica Seles in one of only two matches to be completed in the last two days, found it all a bit much.
"I was more nervous about the curtsy than I was about the match," she admitted. "I said to Monica 'You lead the way and I'll just copy whatever you do.'"
Soggy fun - The rain did little to dampen the spirits of the hardy fanatics who stayed at Wimbledon for the remote chance of watching some tennis.

Although most left when it became clear there was almost no chance of tennis, the few survivors created a good atmosphere on centre and number one courts by singing and watching volunteers from the army playing cricket in the rain with rolled-up umbrellas.

Moth-eaten theory - Why not play under floodlights, thus extending the possible playing hours? Moths are the reason why, according to tournament referee Alan Mills. He says the BBC have told him the moths would flock to the courts from miles around and be a nuisance to both television viewers and the players.
